definition: A winding conductor made of many small insulated copper strands that swap positions along its length and are wrapped together. Large power transformers use it to cut eddy-current losses; few plants make it, so it can hold up large units.
Copper or aluminum wire with a thin enamel or paper insulation, used to wind the coils of transformers and motors. It is the main way copper enters a transformer.
Mineral oil refined from naphthenic crude, the standard insulating and cooling fluid in liquid-filled transformers. It stays fluid in cold weather and resists sludge.

A transformer fluid made from vegetable oil, usually soybean. It is biodegradable and far less flammable than mineral oil, so it is favored near buildings and data centers; Cargill's FR3 is the best-known brand.

Dense cellulose board and kraft paper made from wood pulp, used to insulate and space the windings inside liquid-filled transformers. Large-unit grades come from few suppliers, which makes them a bottleneck.
High-purity aluminum (alloy 1350) made for electrical conductors such as winding strip, foil and cable. It is normally made from primary metal because scrap carries too many impurities.
Cathode is refined copper in sheets from a refinery. Rod mills melt cathode, and some clean scrap, into continuous-cast rod, the feedstock that wire and magnet-wire makers draw down.
Silicon additions used in steelmaking. Electrical steel carries about three percent silicon, which raises its electrical resistance and cuts core losses.

term: Iron ore pellets, pig iron and DRI
definition: The iron sources behind steel: pellets of concentrated ore feed blast furnaces, which make pig iron; DRI and HBI are iron made by direct reduction for electric-arc furnaces. Scrap is the other main input.

Electrical-steel coils are slit into strips and cut into laminations, which are stacked or wound into a transformer core. Core shops sit between steel mills and builders; some builders make cores in-house and others buy them finished.

Small steel balls (shot) or angular particles (grit) thrown at metal to clean and roughen it before painting. Transformer tanks, radiators and enclosures are blasted before coating; Fulton's Metaltec makes these abrasives.
Coating steel with zinc, usually by dipping it in molten zinc, to stop rust. Transmission towers, substation structures and much grid hardware are galvanized, which makes zinc a grid input.
A way to keep buried or submerged steel from corroding by wiring it to a more reactive metal, often zinc or magnesium, that corrodes instead.
Making metal or alloys by melting scrap instead of ore. It uses far less energy than primary production but carries more impurities, which limits it to less demanding grades.

Ways of shaping molten metal. Die casting forces it into steel molds under pressure for zinc and aluminum parts in volume; investment casting pours it into ceramic shells for precise alloy parts; sand casting suits large or low-volume parts.
Cutting metal to precise shapes with computer-controlled mills and lathes. Transformer makers buy machined parts for tap changers, bushings, terminals and tank fittings.

Cutting, forming and welding steel plate into the sealed tank that holds a transformer's core, windings and oil, plus covers and cabinets. Many builders weld tanks in-house; others buy from outside fabricators, a common capacity bottleneck.
Banks of thin steel panels bolted to a liquid-filled transformer's tank; the oil circulates through them to shed heat. Larger units add fans or pumps.

Large power transformers weigh hundreds of tons and move on special rail cars (Schnabel cars, in which the load forms part of the car) or multi-axle road trailers, with permits and route surveys. Few such cars exist, so moves are booked months ahead.
A firm that manages freight for shippers by arranging trucks, warehousing and brokerage. Flatbed trucks carry steel, cable reels and distribution transformers.
Replacing a power line's wires with higher-capacity conductors on the existing towers, a fast way to add transmission capacity. It frees large volumes of scrap aluminum and copper conductor.
Shredding insulated scrap wire and separating the metal from its plastic jacket, producing clean copper or aluminum chops that smelters and rod mills buy.
A long-term contract to buy electricity from a generator at an agreed price. Hyperscalers sign PPAs that fund new plants, which then need step-up transformers and substations.
A data center that rents space, power and cooling to many tenants, unlike a hyperscaler's own campus. Equinix and Digital Realty are the largest operators.
A contractor that designs a project, buys its equipment and builds it under one contract. EPCs such as Quanta, MasTec and Burns & McDonnell buy transformers on behalf of utilities and developers.
A private firm that manages one wealthy family's money. Many invest directly in operating businesses and hold them longer than private-equity funds do.
Investment money with no fixed date for returning cash to investors, unlike a private-equity fund that must sell its companies within roughly a decade. It allows long holds and patient building.

Privately held companies at the small end of the buyout market, often a few million to about a hundred million dollars of revenue (definitions vary). They tend to sell at lower EBITDA multiples than larger companies.
A smaller company bought by an existing portfolio company (the platform) to add products, customers, plants or skills.
The first, usually larger, company bought in a new sector, which later add-ons are merged into.
A US retirement plan that owns company shares for employees. When an ESOP company must buy back shares from retiring workers, the cash strain can lead to a sale, as happened at AFCO.
Debt that ranks below senior bank loans and above equity, carrying higher interest and sometimes equity warrants. It lets buyers fund a deal with less equity.
Another investor that buys a company alongside the lead investor, sharing the equity check and, usually, control.
Buying a business unit, product line or plant that a larger company is selling, rather than a whole company.
A short SEC notice filed when a company raises money privately under an exemption. It shows the amount raised and is often the only public trace of a private deal.
A global code that identifies a legal entity in financial transactions. When a new deal entity registers one, the date can hint at when a transaction happened.

A switch that changes how many turns of a winding are in use, adjusting the transformer's output voltage. On-load tap changers do this while carrying current and are made by very few firms, chiefly Maschinenfabrik Reinhausen and Hitachi Energy.
In the value-chain graph, a box that stands for many smaller firms of the same kind, such as municipal utilities or regional fabricators, when naming each would not fit.
